questions.text:
Use Model One to answer the following questions.

Identify money Flow A on the model.
questions.expectedAnswer: Flow A is Savings — money flowing from Households to the Financial sector.
questions.markingGuide: Correctly identifies Flow A as savings.

questions.text: Explain one reason why money Flow A might decrease in value.
questions.expectedAnswer: If interest rates decrease, households have less incentive to save
questions.markingGuide: Explains a valid reason for decreased savings — e.g., lower interest rates, higher cost of living.

questions.text: Identify one injection into the circular flow model.
questions.expectedAnswer: Any one of: Investment, Government spending/subsidies, Export receipts.

questions.text: Explain one reason why this injection might increase in value.
questions.expectedAnswer: If investment is chosen: lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, encouraging businesses to...
questions.markingGuide: Explains a valid reason for the chosen injection to increase.

questions.text: Explain why economic growth would increase if the Northland trial is successful. Refer to at least two of the flows from Model One in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: A successful Northland trial increases production (income flow from Producers to Households...
questions.markingGuide: Refers to at least two flows and explains how they lead to economic growth.

questions.text: Discuss the impact of a successful trial on the government's operating balance (revenue - expenditure).
questions.expectedAnswer: Revenue increases: more employment means more income tax, more spending means more GST, more...
questions.markingGuide: Discusses both revenue increases and expenditure changes, assessing the net impact on the operating balance.

questions.text: Use the formula for aggregate demand to explain why the purchase of the battery powered aircraft will decrease short-term aggregate demand.
questions.markingGuide: States the AD formula and explains how increased imports decrease AD.

questions.text:
Graph One shows the longer term increase in aggregate demand that results from the increase in consumption spending due to operating the new aircraft.

On Graph One, show the long-term impact of operating the new aircraft on the aggregate supply curve and economic growth.
questions.markingGuide: AS shifted right, correctly labelled. Economic growth shown as increased Real GDP.

questions.text: Referring to Graph One, explain how operating the new aircraft changes aggregate supply.
questions.expectedAnswer: The battery-powered aircraft reduces operating costs (no fuel costs) and increases efficiency
questions.markingGuide: Explains why AS increases — lower costs, increased efficiency, greater productive capacity.

questions.text: Referring to Graph One, explain how operating the new aircraft changes economic growth.
questions.expectedAnswer: Both AD and AS shift right. Real GDP increases from Y to Y1 (or beyond). Economic growth occurs
questions.markingGuide: Explains economic growth as increase in Real GDP with reference to both AD and AS shifts on Graph One.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of the government making it compulsory to use SAF for domestic flights on economic growth and on the environment.
questions.expectedAnswer: Environment benefits: SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel) reduces carbon emissions, improving air...
questions.markingGuide: Compares and contrasts economic growth impacts (short-term cost vs long-term benefit) with environmental impacts (positive).

questions.text:
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of goods and services produced in New Zealand in a year.

Some households buy fruit and vegetables from shops, while others grow their own from seeds they have bought.

How will GDP be affected in the short-term and long-term if more people choose to buy seeds to grow their own fruit and vegetables?

Short-term:
questions.expectedAnswer: Short-term: GDP may increase slightly as people buy seeds, soil, and gardening equipment from...
questions.markingGuide: Identifies that short-term GDP increases due to seed/equipment purchases.

questions.expectedAnswer: Long-term: GDP may decrease as people buy less fruit and vegetables from shops.
questions.markingGuide: Explains that long-term GDP decreases as non-market production replaces market purchases.

questions.text:
Net social welfare is a broad measure of economic growth that uses a combination of economic indicators and quality of life indicators.

Explain one situation when GDP could increase but net social welfare decreases.
questions.expectedAnswer: GDP could increase from factory production that causes pollution.
questions.markingGuide: Identifies a valid scenario — e.g., pollution, overwork, inequality — where GDP rises but welfare falls.

questions.text:
Graph Two and Graph Three show two situations in which economic growth has decreased.

Graph Two: A decrease from A to B (movement along the PPF to a point with fewer consumer goods and fewer capital goods).
Graph Three: A decrease from C to D (movement inside the PPF).

Compare and contrast the causes and effects of the decreases in economic growth shown in Graph Two and Graph Three.

In your answer, explain:
- what could cause the changes shown on the graphs
- which change would be worse for long-term economic growth in New Zealand.
questions.expectedAnswer: Graph Two (A to B): Movement along the PPF
questions.markingGuide: Compares causes (reallocation vs underutilisation) and effects (still efficient vs inefficient). Assesses which is worse for long-term growth with reasoning.
